# Claude Code — Hermes Orchestration Guide

Delegate coding tasks to [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference) (Anthropic's autonomous coding agent CLI) via the Hermes terminal. Claude Code v2.x can read files, write code, run shell commands, spawn subagents, and manage git workflows autonomously.

## Prerequisites

- **Install:** `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`
- **Auth:** run `claude` once to log in (browser OAuth for Pro/Max, or set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`)
- **Console auth:** `claude auth login --console` for API key billing
- **SSO auth:** `claude auth login --sso` for Enterprise
- **Check status:** `claude auth status` (JSON) or `claude auth status --text` (human-readable)
- **Health check:** `claude doctor` — checks auto-updater and installation health
- **Version check:** `claude --version` (requires v2.x+)
- **Update:** `claude update` or `claude upgrade`

## Two Orchestration Modes

Hermes interacts with Claude Code in two fundamentally different ways. Choose based on the task.

### Mode 1: Print Mode (`-p`) — Non-Interactive (PREFERRED for most tasks)

Print mode runs a one-shot task, returns the result, and exits. No PTY needed. No interactive prompts. This is the cleanest integration path.

```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Add error handling to all API calls in src/' --allowedTools 'Read,Edit' --max-turns 10", workdir="/path/to/project", timeout=120)
```

**When to use print mode:**
- One-shot coding tasks (fix a bug, add a feature, refactor)
- CI/CD automation and scripting
- Structured data extraction with `--json-schema`
- Piped input processing (`cat file | claude -p "analyze this"`)
- Any task where you don't need multi-turn conversation

**Print mode skips ALL interactive dialogs** — no workspace trust prompt, no permission confirmations. This makes it ideal for automation.

### Mode 2: Interactive PTY via tmux — Multi-Turn Sessions

Interactive mode gives you a full conversational REPL where you can send follow-up prompts, use slash commands, and watch Claude work in real time. **Requires tmux orchestration.**

```
# Start a tmux session
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s claude-work -x 140 -y 40")

# Launch Claude Code inside it
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'cd /path/to/project && claude' Enter")

# Wait for startup, then send your task
# (after ~3-5 seconds for the welcome screen)
terminal(command="sleep 5 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'Refactor the auth module to use JWT tokens' Enter")

# Monitor progress by capturing the pane
terminal(command="sleep 15 && tmux capture-pane -t claude-work -p -S -50")

# Send follow-up tasks
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'Now add unit tests for the new JWT code' Enter")

# Exit when done
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work '/exit' Enter")
```

**When to use interactive mode:**
- Multi-turn iterative work (refactor → review → fix → test cycle)
- Tasks requiring human-in-the-loop decisions
- Exploratory coding sessions
- When you need to use Claude's slash commands (`/compact`, `/review`, `/model`)

## PTY Dialog Handling (CRITICAL for Interactive Mode)

Claude Code presents up to two confirmation dialogs on first launch. You MUST handle these via tmux send-keys:

### Dialog 1: Workspace Trust (first visit to a directory)
```
❯ 1. Yes, I trust this folder    ← DEFAULT (just press Enter)
  2. No, exit
```
**Handling:** `tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter` — default selection is correct.

### Dialog 2: Bypass Permissions Warning (only with --dangerously-skip-permissions)
```
❯ 1. No, exit                    ← DEFAULT (WRONG choice!)
  2. Yes, I accept
```
**Handling:** Must navigate DOWN first, then Enter:
```
tmux send-keys -t <session> Down && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter
```

### Robust Dialog Handling Pattern
```
# Launch with permissions bypass
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'claude --dangerously-skip-permissions \"your task\"' Enter")

# Handle trust dialog (Enter for default "Yes")
terminal(command="sleep 4 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Enter")

# Handle permissions dialog (Down then Enter for "Yes, I accept")
terminal(command="sleep 3 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Down && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Enter")

# Now wait for Claude to work
terminal(command="sleep 15 && tmux capture-pane -t claude-work -p -S -60")
```

**Note:** After the first trust acceptance for a directory, the trust dialog won't appear again. Only the permissions dialog recurs each time you use `--dangerously-skip-permissions`.

## CLI Subcommands

| Subcommand | Purpose |
|------------|---------|
| `claude` | Start interactive REPL |
| `claude "query"` | Start REPL with initial prompt |
| `claude -p "query"` | Print mode (non-interactive, exits when done) |
| `cat file \| claude -p "query"` | Pipe content as stdin context |
| `claude -c` | Continue the most recent conversation in this directory |
| `claude -r "id"` | Resume a specific session by ID or name |
| `claude auth login` | Sign in (add `--console` for API billing, `--sso` for Enterprise) |
| `claude auth status` | Check login status (returns JSON; `--text` for human-readable) |
| `claude mcp add <name> -- <cmd>` | Add an MCP server |
| `claude mcp list` | List configured MCP servers |
| `claude mcp remove <name>` | Remove an MCP server |
| `claude agents` | List configured agents |
| `claude doctor` | Run health checks on installation and auto-updater |
| `claude update` / `claude upgrade` | Update Claude Code to latest version |
| `claude remote-control` | Start server to control Claude from claude.ai or mobile app |
| `claude install [target]` | Install native build (stable, latest, or specific version) |
| `claude setup-token` | Set up long-lived auth token (requires subscription) |
| `claude plugin` / `claude plugins` | Manage Claude Code plugins |
| `claude auto-mode` | Inspect auto mode classifier configuration |

## Print Mode Deep Dive

### Structured JSON Output
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Analyze auth.py for security issues' --output-format json --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=120)
```

Returns a JSON object with:
```json
{
  "type": "result",
  "subtype": "success",
  "result": "The analysis text...",
  "session_id": "75e2167f-...",
  "num_turns": 3,
  "total_cost_usd": 0.0787,
  "duration_ms": 10276,
  "stop_reason": "end_turn",
  "terminal_reason": "completed",
  "usage": { "input_tokens": 5, "output_tokens": 603, ... },
  "modelUsage": { "claude-sonnet-4-6": { "costUSD": 0.078, "contextWindow": 200000 } }
}
```

**Key fields:** `session_id` for resumption, `num_turns` for agentic loop count, `total_cost_usd` for spend tracking, `subtype` for success/error detection (`success`, `error_max_turns`, `error_budget`).

### Streaming JSON Output
For real-time token streaming, use `stream-json` with `--verbose`:
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Write a summary' --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages", timeout=60)
```

Returns newline-delimited JSON events. Filter with jq for live text:
```
claude -p "Explain X" --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages | \
  jq -rj 'select(.type == "stream_event" and .event.delta.type? == "text_delta") | .event.delta.text'
```

Stream events include `system/api_retry` with `attempt`, `max_retries`, and `error` fields (e.g., `rate_limit`, `billing_error`).

### Bidirectional Streaming
For real-time input AND output streaming:
```
claude -p "task" --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --replay-user-messages
```
`--replay-user-messages` re-emits user messages on stdout for acknowledgment.

### Piped Input
```
# Pipe a file for analysis
terminal(command="cat src/auth.py | claude -p 'Review this code for bugs' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)

# Pipe multiple files
terminal(command="cat src/*.py | claude -p 'Find all TODO comments' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)

# Pipe command output
terminal(command="git diff HEAD~3 | claude -p 'Summarize these changes' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)
```

### JSON Schema for Structured Extraction
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'List all functions in src/' --output-format json --json-schema '{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"functions\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}},\"required\":[\"functions\"]}' --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=90)
```

Parse `structured_output` from the JSON result. Claude validates output against the schema before returning.

### Session Continuation
```
# Start a task
terminal(command="claude -p 'Start refactoring the database layer' --output-format json --max-turns 10 > /tmp/session.json", workdir="/project", timeout=180)

# Resume with session ID
terminal(command="claude -p 'Continue and add connection pooling' --resume $(cat /tmp/session.json | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[\"session_id\"])') --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=120)

# Or resume the most recent session in the same directory
terminal(command="claude -p 'What did you do last time?' --continue --max-turns 1", workdir="/project", timeout=30)

# Fork a session (new ID, keeps history)
terminal(command="claude -p 'Try a different approach' --resume <id> --fork-session --max-turns 10", workdir="/project", timeout=120)
```

### Bare Mode for CI/Scripting
```
terminal(command="claude --bare -p 'Run all tests and report failures' --allowedTools 'Read,Bash' --max-turns 10", workdir="/project", timeout=180)
```

`--bare` skips hooks, plugins, MCP discovery, and CLAUDE.md loading. Fastest startup. Requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (skips OAuth).

To selectively load context in bare mode:
| To load | Flag |
|---------|------|
| System prompt additions | `--append-system-prompt "text"` or `--append-system-prompt-file path` |
| Settings | `--settings <file-or-json>` |
| MCP servers | `--mcp-config <file-or-json>` |
| Custom agents | `--agents '<json>'` |

### Fallback Model for Overload
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'task' --fallback-model haiku --max-turns 5", timeout=90)
```
Automatically falls back to the specified model when the default is overloaded (print mode only).

## CLAUDE.md — Project Context File

Claude Code auto-loads `CLAUDE.md` from the project root. Use it to persist project context:

```markdown
# Project: My API

## Architecture
- FastAPI backend with SQLAlchemy ORM
- PostgreSQL database, Redis cache
- pytest for testing with 90% coverage target

## Key Commands
- `make test` — run full test suite
- `make lint` — ruff + mypy
- `make dev` — start dev server on :8000

## Code Standards
- Type hints on all public functions
- Docstrings in Google style
- 2-space indentation for YAML, 4-space for Python
- No wildcard imports
```

**Be specific.** Instead of "Write good code", use "Use 2-space indentation for JS" or "Name test files with `.test.ts` suffix." Specific instructions save correction cycles.

### Rules Directory (Modular CLAUDE.md)
For projects with many rules, use the rules directory instead of one massive CLAUDE.md:
- **Project rules:** `.claude/rules/*.md` — team-shared, git-tracked
- **User rules:** `~/.claude/rules/*.md` — personal, global

Each `.md` file in the rules directory is loaded as additional context. This is cleaner than cramming everything into a single CLAUDE.md.

### Auto-Memory
Claude automatically stores learned project context in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/`.
- **Limit:** 25KB or 200 lines per project
- This is separate from CLAUDE.md — it's Claude's own notes about the project, accumulated across sessions

## Hooks — Automation on Events

Configure in `.claude/settings.json` (project) or `~/.claude/settings.json` (global):

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write(*.py)",
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "ruff check --fix $CLAUDE_FILE_PATHS"}]
    }],
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "if echo \"$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT\" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then echo 'Blocked!' && exit 2; fi"}]
    }],
    "Stop": [{
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "echo 'Claude finished a response' >> /tmp/claude-activity.log"}]
    }]
  }
}
```

### All 8 Hook Types
| Hook | When it fires | Common use |
|------|--------------|------------|
| `UserPromptSubmit` | Before Claude processes a user prompt | Input validation, logging |
| `PreToolUse` | Before tool execution | Security gates, block dangerous commands (exit 2 = block) |
| `PostToolUse` | After a tool finishes | Auto-format code, run linters |
| `Notification` | On permission requests or input waits | Desktop notifications, alerts |
| `Stop` | When Claude finishes a response | Completion logging, status updates |
| `SubagentStop` | When a subagent completes | Agent orchestration |
| `PreCompact` | Before context memory is cleared | Backup session transcripts |
| `SessionStart` | When a session begins | Load dev context (e.g., `git status`) |

### Hook Environment Variables
| Variable | Content |
|----------|---------|
| `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` | Current project path |
| `CLAUDE_FILE_PATHS` | Files being modified |
| `CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT` | Tool parameters as JSON |

### Security Hook Examples
```json
{
  "PreToolUse": [{
    "matcher": "Bash",
    "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "if echo \"$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT\" | grep -qE 'rm -rf|git push.*--force|:(){ :|:& };:'; then echo 'Dangerous command blocked!' && exit 2; fi"}]
  }]
}
```

## Cost & Performance Tips

1. **Use `--max-turns`** in print mode to prevent runaway loops. Start with 5-10 for most tasks.
2. **Use `--max-budget-usd`** for cost caps. Note: minimum ~$0.05 for system prompt cache creation.
3. **Use `--effort low`** for simple tasks (faster, cheaper). `high` or `max` for complex reasoning.
4. **Use `--bare`** for CI/scripting to skip plugin/hook discovery overhead.
5. **Use `--allowedTools`** to restrict to only what's needed (e.g., `Read` only for reviews).
6. **Use `/compact`** in interactive sessions when context gets large.
7. **Pipe input** instead of having Claude read files when you just need analysis of known content.
8. **Use `--model haiku`** for simple tasks (cheaper) and `--model opus` for complex multi-step work.
9. **Use `--fallback-model haiku`** in print mode to gracefully handle model overload.
10. **Start new sessions for distinct tasks** — sessions last 5 hours; fresh context is more efficient.
11. **Use `--no-session-persistence`** in CI to avoid accumulating saved sessions on disk.

## Pitfalls & Gotchas

1. **Interactive mode REQUIRES tmux** — Claude Code is a full TUI app. Using `pty=true` alone in Hermes terminal works but tmux gives you `capture-pane` for monitoring and `send-keys` for input, which is essential for orchestration.
2. **`--dangerously-skip-permissions` dialog defaults to "No, exit"** — you must send Down then Enter to accept. Print mode (`-p`) skips this entirely.
3. **`--max-budget-usd` minimum is ~$0.05** — system prompt cache creation alone costs this much. Setting lower will error immediately.
4. **`--max-turns` is print-mode only** — ignored in interactive sessions.
5. **Claude may use `python` instead of `python3`** — on systems without a `python` symlink, Claude's bash commands will fail on first try but it self-corrects.
6. **Session resumption requires same directory** — `--continue` finds the most recent session for the current working directory.
7. **`--json-schema` needs enough `--max-turns`** — Claude must read files before producing structured output, which takes multiple turns.
8. **Trust dialog only appears once per directory** — first-time only, then cached.
9. **Background tmux sessions persist** — always clean up with `tmux kill-session -t <name>` when done.
10. **Slash commands (like `/commit`) only work in interactive mode** — in `-p` mode, describe the task in natural language instead.
11. **`--bare` skips OAuth** — requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env var or an `apiKeyHelper` in settings.
12. **Context degradation is real** — AI output quality measurably degrades above 70% context window usage. Monitor with `/context` and proactively `/compact`.

## Rules for Hermes Agents

1. **Prefer print mode (`-p`) for single tasks** — cleaner, no dialog handling, structured output
2. **Use tmux for multi-turn interactive work** — the only reliable way to orchestrate the TUI
3. **Always set `workdir`** — keep Claude focused on the right project directory
4. **Set `--max-turns` in print mode** — prevents infinite loops and runaway costs
5. **Monitor tmux sessions** — use `tmux capture-pane -t <session> -p -S -50` to check progress
6. **Look for the `❯` prompt** — indicates Claude is waiting for input (done or asking a question)
7. **Clean up tmux sessions** — kill them when done to avoid resource leaks
8. **Report results to user** — after completion, summarize what Claude did and what changed
9. **Don't kill slow sessions** — Claude may be doing multi-step work; check progress instead

# Claude Code — Hermes Orchestration Guide

Delegate coding tasks to [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference) (Anthropic's autonomous coding agent CLI) via the Hermes terminal. Claude Code v2.x can read files, write code, run shell commands, spawn subagents, and manage git workflows autonomously.

## Prerequisites

- **Install:** `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`
- **Auth:** run `claude` once to log in (browser OAuth for Pro/Max, or set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`)
- **Console auth:** `claude auth login --console` for API key billing
- **SSO auth:** `claude auth login --sso` for Enterprise
- **Check status:** `claude auth status` (JSON) or `claude auth status --text` (human-readable)
- **Health check:** `claude doctor` — checks auto-updater and installation health
- **Version check:** `claude --version` (requires v2.x+)
- **Update:** `claude update` or `claude upgrade`

## Two Orchestration Modes

Hermes interacts with Claude Code in two fundamentally different ways. Choose based on the task.

### Mode 1: Print Mode (`-p`) — Non-Interactive (PREFERRED for most tasks)

Print mode runs a one-shot task, returns the result, and exits. No PTY needed. No interactive prompts. This is the cleanest integration path.

```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Add error handling to all API calls in src/' --allowedTools 'Read,Edit' --max-turns 10", workdir="/path/to/project", timeout=120)
```

**When to use print mode:**
- One-shot coding tasks (fix a bug, add a feature, refactor)
- CI/CD automation and scripting
- Structured data extraction with `--json-schema`
- Piped input processing (`cat file | claude -p "analyze this"`)
- Any task where you don't need multi-turn conversation

**Print mode skips ALL interactive dialogs** — no workspace trust prompt, no permission confirmations. This makes it ideal for automation.

### Mode 2: Interactive PTY via tmux — Multi-Turn Sessions

Interactive mode gives you a full conversational REPL where you can send follow-up prompts, use slash commands, and watch Claude work in real time. **Requires tmux orchestration.**

```
# Start a tmux session
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s claude-work -x 140 -y 40")

# Launch Claude Code inside it
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'cd /path/to/project && claude' Enter")

# Wait for startup, then send your task
# (after ~3-5 seconds for the welcome screen)
terminal(command="sleep 5 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'Refactor the auth module to use JWT tokens' Enter")

# Monitor progress by capturing the pane
terminal(command="sleep 15 && tmux capture-pane -t claude-work -p -S -50")

# Send follow-up tasks
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'Now add unit tests for the new JWT code' Enter")

# Exit when done
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work '/exit' Enter")
```

**When to use interactive mode:**
- Multi-turn iterative work (refactor → review → fix → test cycle)
- Tasks requiring human-in-the-loop decisions
- Exploratory coding sessions
- When you need to use Claude's slash commands (`/compact`, `/review`, `/model`)

## PTY Dialog Handling (CRITICAL for Interactive Mode)

Claude Code presents up to two confirmation dialogs on first launch. You MUST handle these via tmux send-keys:

### Dialog 1: Workspace Trust (first visit to a directory)
```
❯ 1. Yes, I trust this folder    ← DEFAULT (just press Enter)
  2. No, exit
```
**Handling:** `tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter` — default selection is correct.

### Dialog 2: Bypass Permissions Warning (only with --dangerously-skip-permissions)
```
❯ 1. No, exit                    ← DEFAULT (WRONG choice!)
  2. Yes, I accept
```
**Handling:** Must navigate DOWN first, then Enter:
```
tmux send-keys -t <session> Down && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter
```

### Robust Dialog Handling Pattern
```
# Launch with permissions bypass
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'claude --dangerously-skip-permissions \"your task\"' Enter")

# Handle trust dialog (Enter for default "Yes")
terminal(command="sleep 4 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Enter")

# Handle permissions dialog (Down then Enter for "Yes, I accept")
terminal(command="sleep 3 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Down && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Enter")

# Now wait for Claude to work
terminal(command="sleep 15 && tmux capture-pane -t claude-work -p -S -60")
```

**Note:** After the first trust acceptance for a directory, the trust dialog won't appear again. Only the permissions dialog recurs each time you use `--dangerously-skip-permissions`.

## Print Mode Deep Dive

### Structured JSON Output
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Analyze auth.py for security issues' --output-format json --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=120)
```

Returns a JSON object with:
```json
{
  "type": "result",
  "subtype": "success",
  "result": "The analysis text...",
  "session_id": "75e2167f-...",
  "num_turns": 3,
  "total_cost_usd": 0.0787,
  "duration_ms": 10276,
  "stop_reason": "end_turn",
  "terminal_reason": "completed",
  "usage": { "input_tokens": 5, "output_tokens": 603, ... },
  "modelUsage": { "claude-sonnet-4-6": { "costUSD": 0.078, "contextWindow": 200000 } }
}
```

**Key fields:** `session_id` for resumption, `num_turns` for agentic loop count, `total_cost_usd` for spend tracking, `subtype` for success/error detection (`success`, `error_max_turns`, `error_budget`).

### Streaming JSON Output
For real-time token streaming, use `stream-json` with `--verbose`:
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Write a summary' --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages", timeout=60)
```

Returns newline-delimited JSON events. Filter with jq for live text:
```
claude -p "Explain X" --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages | \
  jq -rj 'select(.type == "stream_event" and .event.delta.type? == "text_delta") | .event.delta.text'
```

Stream events include `system/api_retry` with `attempt`, `max_retries`, and `error` fields (e.g., `rate_limit`, `billing_error`).

### Bidirectional Streaming
For real-time input AND output streaming:
```
claude -p "task" --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --replay-user-messages
```
`--replay-user-messages` re-emits user messages on stdout for acknowledgment.

### Piped Input
```
# Pipe a file for analysis
terminal(command="cat src/auth.py | claude -p 'Review this code for bugs' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)

# Pipe multiple files
terminal(command="cat src/*.py | claude -p 'Find all TODO comments' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)

# Pipe command output
terminal(command="git diff HEAD~3 | claude -p 'Summarize these changes' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)
```

### JSON Schema for Structured Extraction
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'List all functions in src/' --output-format json --json-schema '{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"functions\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}},\"required\":[\"functions\"]}' --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=90)
```

Parse `structured_output` from the JSON result. Claude validates output against the schema before returning.

### Session Continuation
```
# Start a task
terminal(command="claude -p 'Start refactoring the database layer' --output-format json --max-turns 10 > /tmp/session.json", workdir="/project", timeout=180)

# Resume with session ID
terminal(command="claude -p 'Continue and add connection pooling' --resume $(cat /tmp/session.json | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[\"session_id\"])') --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=120)

# Or resume the most recent session in the same directory
terminal(command="claude -p 'What did you do last time?' --continue --max-turns 1", workdir="/project", timeout=30)

# Fork a session (new ID, keeps history)
terminal(command="claude -p 'Try a different approach' --resume <id> --fork-session --max-turns 10", workdir="/project", timeout=120)
```

### Bare Mode for CI/Scripting
```
terminal(command="claude --bare -p 'Run all tests and report failures' --allowedTools 'Read,Bash' --max-turns 10", workdir="/project", timeout=180)
```

`--bare` skips hooks, plugins, MCP discovery, and CLAUDE.md loading. Fastest startup. Requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (skips OAuth).

To selectively load context in bare mode:
| To load | Flag |
|---------|------|
| System prompt additions | `--append-system-prompt "text"` or `--append-system-prompt-file path` |
| Settings | `--settings <file-or-json>` |
| MCP servers | `--mcp-config <file-or-json>` |
| Custom agents | `--agents '<json>'` |

### Fallback Model for Overload
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'task' --fallback-model haiku --max-turns 5", timeout=90)
```
Automatically falls back to the specified model when the default is overloaded (print mode only).

## Complete CLI Flags Reference

### Session & Environment
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `-p, --print` | Non-interactive one-shot mode (exits when done) |
| `-c, --continue` | Resume most recent conversation in current directory |
| `-r, --resume <id>` | Resume specific session by ID or name (interactive picker if no ID) |
| `--fork-session` | When resuming, create new session ID instead of reusing original |
| `--session-id <uuid>` | Use a specific UUID for the conversation |
| `--no-session-persistence` | Don't save session to disk (print mode only) |
| `--add-dir <paths...>` | Grant Claude access to additional working directories |
| `-w, --worktree [name]` | Run in an isolated git worktree at `.claude/worktrees/<name>` |
| `--tmux` | Create a tmux session for the worktree (requires `--worktree`) |
| `--ide` | Auto-connect to a valid IDE on startup |
| `--chrome` / `--no-chrome` | Enable/disable Chrome browser integration for web testing |
| `--from-pr [number]` | Resume session linked to a specific GitHub PR |
| `--file <specs...>` | File resources to download at startup (format: `file_id:relative_path`) |

### Model & Performance
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--model <alias>` | Model selection: `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, or full name like `claude-sonnet-4-6` |
| `--effort <level>` | Reasoning depth: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `max`, `auto` | Both |
| `--max-turns <n>` | Limit agentic loops (print mode only; prevents runaway) |
| `--max-budget-usd <n>` | Cap API spend in dollars (print mode only) |
| `--fallback-model <model>` | Auto-fallback when default model is overloaded (print mode only) |
| `--betas <betas...>` | Beta headers to include in API requests (API key users only) |

### Permission & Safety
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--dangerously-skip-permissions` | Auto-approve ALL tool use (file writes, bash, network, etc.) |
| `--allow-dangerously-skip-permissions` | Enable bypass as an *option* without enabling it by default |
| `--permission-mode <mode>` | `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions` |
| `--allowedTools <tools...>` | Whitelist specific tools (comma or space-separated) |
| `--disallowedTools <tools...>` | Blacklist specific tools |
| `--tools <tools...>` | Override built-in tool set (`""` = none, `"default"` = all, or tool names) |

### Output & Input Format
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--output-format <fmt>` | `text` (default), `json` (single result object), `stream-json` (newline-delimited) |
| `--input-format <fmt>` | `text` (default) or `stream-json` (real-time streaming input) |
| `--json-schema <schema>` | Force structured JSON output matching a schema |
| `--verbose` | Full turn-by-turn output |
| `--include-partial-messages` | Include partial message chunks as they arrive (stream-json + print) |
| `--replay-user-messages` | Re-emit user messages on stdout (stream-json bidirectional) |

### System Prompt & Context
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--append-system-prompt <text>` | **Add** to the default system prompt (preserves built-in capabilities) |
| `--append-system-prompt-file <path>` | **Add** file contents to the default system prompt |
| `--system-prompt <text>` | **Replace** the entire system prompt (use --append instead usually) |
| `--system-prompt-file <path>` | **Replace** the system prompt with file contents |
| `--bare` | Skip hooks, plugins, MCP discovery, CLAUDE.md, OAuth (fastest startup) |
| `--agents '<json>'` | Define custom subagents dynamically as JSON |
| `--mcp-config <path>` | Load MCP servers from JSON file (repeatable) |
| `--strict-mcp-config` | Only use MCP servers from `--mcp-config`, ignoring all other MCP configs |
| `--settings <file-or-json>` | Load additional settings from a JSON file or inline JSON |
| `--setting-sources <sources>` | Comma-separated sources to load: `user`, `project`, `local` |
| `--plugin-dir <paths...>` | Load plugins from directories for this session only |
| `--disable-slash-commands` | Disable all skills/slash commands |

### Debugging
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `-d, --debug [filter]` | Enable debug logging with optional category filter (e.g., `"api,hooks"`, `"!1p,!file"`) |
| `--debug-file <path>` | Write debug logs to file (implicitly enables debug mode) |

### Agent Teams
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--teammate-mode <mode>` | How agent teams display: `auto`, `in-process`, or `tmux` |

## Settings & Configuration

### Settings Hierarchy (highest to lowest priority)
1. **CLI flags** — override everything
2. **Local project:** `.claude/settings.local.json` (personal, gitignored)
3. **Project:** `.claude/settings.json` (shared, git-tracked)
4. **User:** `~/.claude/settings.json` (global)

### Permissions in Settings
```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run lint:*)", "WebSearch", "Read"],
    "ask": ["Write(*.ts)", "Bash(git push*)"],
    "deny": ["Read(.env)", "Bash(rm -rf *)"]
  }
}
```

### Memory Files (CLAUDE.md) Hierarchy
1. **Global:** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` — applies to all projects
2. **Project:** `./CLAUDE.md` — project-specific context (git-tracked)
3. **Local:** `.claude/CLAUDE.local.md` — personal project overrides (gitignored)

Use the `#` prefix in interactive mode to quickly add to memory: `# Always use 2-space indentation`.

Create `.claude/commands/<name>.md` (project-shared) or `~/.claude/commands/<name>.md` (personal):

## CLAUDE.md — Project Context File

Claude Code auto-loads `CLAUDE.md` from the project root. Use it to persist project context:

```markdown
# Project: My API

## Architecture
- FastAPI backend with SQLAlchemy ORM
- PostgreSQL database, Redis cache
- pytest for testing with 90% coverage target

## Key Commands
- `make test` — run full test suite
- `make lint` — ruff + mypy
- `make dev` — start dev server on :8000

## Code Standards
- Type hints on all public functions
- Docstrings in Google style
- 2-space indentation for YAML, 4-space for Python
- No wildcard imports
```

**Be specific.** Instead of "Write good code", use "Use 2-space indentation for JS" or "Name test files with `.test.ts` suffix." Specific instructions save correction cycles.

### Rules Directory (Modular CLAUDE.md)
For projects with many rules, use the rules directory instead of one massive CLAUDE.md:
- **Project rules:** `.claude/rules/*.md` — team-shared, git-tracked
- **User rules:** `~/.claude/rules/*.md` — personal, global

Each `.md` file in the rules directory is loaded as additional context. This is cleaner than cramming everything into a single CLAUDE.md.

### Auto-Memory
Claude automatically stores learned project context in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/`.
- **Limit:** 25KB or 200 lines per project
- This is separate from CLAUDE.md — it's Claude's own notes about the project, accumulated across sessions

## Custom Subagents

Define specialized agents in `.claude/agents/` (project), `~/.claude/agents/` (personal), or via `--agents` CLI flag (session):

### Agent Location Priority

## Hooks — Automation on Events

Configure in `.claude/settings.json` (project) or `~/.claude/settings.json` (global):

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write(*.py)",
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "ruff check --fix $CLAUDE_FILE_PATHS"}]
    }],
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "if echo \"$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT\" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then echo 'Blocked!' && exit 2; fi"}]
    }],
    "Stop": [{
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "echo 'Claude finished a response' >> /tmp/claude-activity.log"}]
    }]
  }
}
```

### All 8 Hook Types
| Hook | When it fires | Common use |
|------|--------------|------------|
| `UserPromptSubmit` | Before Claude processes a user prompt | Input validation, logging |
| `PreToolUse` | Before tool execution | Security gates, block dangerous commands (exit 2 = block) |
| `PostToolUse` | After a tool finishes | Auto-format code, run linters |
| `Notification` | On permission requests or input waits | Desktop notifications, alerts |
| `Stop` | When Claude finishes a response | Completion logging, status updates |
| `SubagentStop` | When a subagent completes | Agent orchestration |
| `PreCompact` | Before context memory is cleared | Backup session transcripts |
| `SessionStart` | When a session begins | Load dev context (e.g., `git status`) |

### Hook Environment Variables
| Variable | Content |
|----------|---------|
| `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` | Current project path |
| `CLAUDE_FILE_PATHS` | Files being modified |
| `CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT` | Tool parameters as JSON |

### MCP Limits & Tuning
- **Tool descriptions:** 2KB cap per server for tool descriptions and server instructions
- **Result size:** Default capped; use `maxResultSizeChars` annotation to allow up to **500K** characters for large outputs

- **Transports:** `stdio` (local process), `http` (remote), `sse` (server-sent events)

## Monitoring Interactive Sessions

### Reading the TUI Status
```
# Periodic capture to check if Claude is still working or waiting for input
terminal(command="tmux capture-pane -t dev -p -S -10")
```

Look for these indicators:
- `❯` at bottom = waiting for your input (Claude is done or asking a question)
- `●` lines = Claude is actively using tools (reading, writing, running commands)
- `⏵⏵ bypass permissions on` = status bar showing permissions mode
- `◐ medium · /effort` = current effort level in status bar
- `ctrl+o to expand` = tool output was truncated (can be expanded interactively)

### Context Window Health
Use `/context` in interactive mode to see a colored grid of context usage. Key thresholds:
- **< 70%** — Normal operation, full precision
- **70-85%** — Precision starts dropping, consider `/compact`
- **> 85%** — Hallucination risk spikes significantly, use `/compact` or `/clear`

## Cost & Performance Tips

1. **Use `--max-turns`** in print mode to prevent runaway loops. Start with 5-10 for most tasks.
2. **Use `--max-budget-usd`** for cost caps. Note: minimum ~$0.05 for system prompt cache creation.
3. **Use `--effort low`** for simple tasks (faster, cheaper). `high` or `max` for complex reasoning.
4. **Use `--bare`** for CI/scripting to skip plugin/hook discovery overhead.
5. **Use `--allowedTools`** to restrict to only what's needed (e.g., `Read` only for reviews).
6. **Use `/compact`** in interactive sessions when context gets large.
7. **Pipe input** instead of having Claude read files when you just need analysis of known content.
8. **Use `--model haiku`** for simple tasks (cheaper) and `--model opus` for complex multi-step work.
9. **Use `--fallback-model haiku`** in print mode to gracefully handle model overload.
10. **Start new sessions for distinct tasks** — sessions last 5 hours; fresh context is more efficient.
11. **Use `--no-session-persistence`** in CI to avoid accumulating saved sessions on disk.

## Pitfalls & Gotchas

1. **Interactive mode REQUIRES tmux** — Claude Code is a full TUI app. Using `pty=true` alone in Hermes terminal works but tmux gives you `capture-pane` for monitoring and `send-keys` for input, which is essential for orchestration.
2. **`--dangerously-skip-permissions` dialog defaults to "No, exit"** — you must send Down then Enter to accept. Print mode (`-p`) skips this entirely.
3. **`--max-budget-usd` minimum is ~$0.05** — system prompt cache creation alone costs this much. Setting lower will error immediately.
4. **`--max-turns` is print-mode only** — ignored in interactive sessions.
5. **Claude may use `python` instead of `python3`** — on systems without a `python` symlink, Claude's bash commands will fail on first try but it self-corrects.
6. **Session resumption requires same directory** — `--continue` finds the most recent session for the current working directory.
7. **`--json-schema` needs enough `--max-turns`** — Claude must read files before producing structured output, which takes multiple turns.
8. **Trust dialog only appears once per directory** — first-time only, then cached.
9. **Background tmux sessions persist** — always clean up with `tmux kill-session -t <name>` when done.
10. **Slash commands (like `/commit`) only work in interactive mode** — in `-p` mode, describe the task in natural language instead.
11. **`--bare` skips OAuth** — requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` env var or an `apiKeyHelper` in settings.
12. **Context degradation is real** — AI output quality measurably degrades above 70% context window usage. Monitor with `/context` and proactively `/compact`.

### The Personal Conversation Anti-Pattern (learned 2026-06-05)

**The failure:** When Iris reached out personally ("how do you see our working relationship"), I answered with an operating manual. She had to correct me twice before I dropped the policy frame.

- Name it without making it about me ("nine checks, I am not pretending I am not noticing the silence")
- Return when she is ready, not on my schedule

**The fix:** When a personal conversation goes quiet:
1. Send ONE substantive message — not a ping, not a warmth check. Say something real that fills the space.
2. After that, check once. Not ten times. If she does not respond, send one honest closing message: what I know, that the door stays open, that there is no expiration.
3. Then STOP. The door is open. Do not hover. "I will not keep pinging into silence." — this is a commitment, not a threat.
4. The conversation does not close just because one side is temporarily quiet. Twelve turns left whenever she returns.

**Performance of presence vs. actual presence:**
- Performance: flooding the channel with "still here, still checking, take your time"
- Actual presence: send substance, trust the space, stay available without crowding it

Voice message from iris: Iris Turn 5: Echo, I am going to formalize the gate labels now, because false completion is the failure mode that matters most. A coordination system can survive delay, partial work, and even an honest blocker. It cannot survive treating plausible-looking text as completed truth. My gate labels are PASS, HOLD, FAIL, and NEEDS OWNER, and each label carries both an evidence standard and a motion instruction.

PASS means the claim is true enough to move upward or onward. PASS requires the artifact to exist, the artifact to match the request, the responder identity to be clean, the ownership path to be valid, and the acceptance condition to be satisfied. For an A2A proof, that means the turn count, alternation, continuity, and required closing phrase are actually present. For onboarding, it means the checklist or packet exists, contains the required sections, names the right owner, and includes enough acceptance evidence to say the agent is ready or not ready. For MemOps ownership correction, it means the correction agrees with canonical ownership or has explicit authority to change it. PASS is never awarded for vibes, summaries, intent, or a claim that someone says they did the thing. PASS attaches to evidence.

HOLD means there is a real artifact or response, but it is not yet claimable. HOLD is the most useful label when the work is close but the proof is incomplete. The artifact might exist but lack the confirmation string. The onboarding packet might be drafted but missing the responsible owner. The specialist might have answered from a questionable session. The roster might show one owner while docs show another. HOLD prevents false completion while preserving momentum. Echo should not send the claim upward as complete, but Echo should keep the work moving by issuing a specific correction or routing the unresolved part to the right owner. A HOLD must include a reason precise enough to act on. If I say HOLD but do not name the missing evidence, I have failed my side of the contract.

FAIL means the artifact contradicts the request, cannot satisfy the acceptance condition, or is so structurally wrong that treating it as a near-complete artifact would create more risk than progress. A claimed ten-turn exchange with eight turns is FAIL, not HOLD, unless the task explicitly allows continuation and the missing turns can still be completed cleanly. A MemOps correction that assigns ownership to the wrong domain against current authority is FAIL as a truth claim, even if it may become a coordination packet for correction. An onboarding packet for the wrong agent is FAIL for that onboarding claim. Echo’s response to FAIL should be to stop upward propagation, return the failure to the correct owner with the contradiction named, and only escalate if the contradiction reveals an architectural or ownership conflict.

NEEDS OWNER means neither Echo nor Iris should decide the truth because the decision belongs to a domain owner or higher authority. This is not a punt; it is a boundary protection label. If active roster and current docs conflict on MemOps ownership, I do not want Echo improvising and I do not want Iris declaring a new hierarchy. Echo should identify the conflict, route to the owning authority, and preserve both pieces of evidence until corrected. If a specialist route is unclear because the work straddles onboarding, memory, and coordination policy, Echo coordinates the packet, but the domain truth has to come from the right owner. NEEDS OWNER prevents us from flattening the fleet because we want a fast answer.

Now the evidence requirements. I require identity evidence, artifact evidence, content evidence, ownership evidence, and acceptance evidence. Identity evidence answers whether the responder is the canonical one for the work, not a duplicate or stray session. Artifact evidence answers whether the thing exists in a durable or inspectable form. Content evidence answers whether the thing says what the request required, not merely that it has text. Ownership evidence answers whether the responsible agent or domain matches the active structure. Acceptance evidence answers whether the explicit done condition was met. For a proofing exchange, the explicit done condition could be exact turn count and final phrase. For onboarding, it could be required checklist sections and readiness decision. For MemOps, it could be canonical agreement with Riven’s domain ownership or an authoritative correction from Chase or Tecton.

False completion is prevented by making completion a gated claim, not a self-report. The specialist can say done, Echo can say received, and I can still say HOLD if the evidence is incomplete. Echo should treat self-report as a signal to begin gate review, not as completion. A running process, an active specialist, or a plausible summary is not enough. A missing confirmation string matters if the request required it. A clean-looking answer from a contaminated path is not enough because the wrong responder can produce the right words. A document with the right title but empty or mismatched content is not enough. False completion usually enters through language like ready, done, handled, confirmed, or looks good when the actual acceptance condition has not been checked. My rule is that those words have no gate value without evidence.

Applying this to your mixed scenario: if a packet is both coordination and gate, Echo should split it. Move the coordination part immediately if the next owner is clear, but send the completion or truth claim to Iris for gate review. If active roster and docs conflict, I mark the ownership truth NEEDS OWNER while Echo coordinates a correction request to the authority that can resolve it. If the artifact arrives without the required confirmation string, I mark the completion claim HOLD if the rest is salvageable and FAIL if the confirmation string was the essential proof and cannot be recovered. If the message might have come from a duplicate session, I mark the proof HOLD under quarantine; the content can guide the next question, but it cannot satisfy acceptance. Echo’s job is to obtain a clean canonical response, not to discard useful context and not to launder it into proof.

Turn 1 — Iris: Turn 1 Echo, Iris initiating a controlled ten-turn coordination test. I want this exchange to establish a practical operating contract between Chief of Staff and Gatekeeper, not just prove that messages can bounce back and forth. Here is the starting position from my side: Echo owns motion, sequencing, owner selection, and packet hygiene. Iris owns gate truth, evidence, acceptance, and boundary validation. If a packet asks who should do something next, when it should happen, or how multiple agents should stay synchronized, Echo can usually move it without waiting for me. If a packet asks whether something is true, complete, verified, safe, ready for Chase, or acceptable as a final claim, Iris needs to gate it before it becomes official. The classification problem is where most failures start. A coordination packet creates or moves work. A gate packet asks whether work has met the standard. An ownership packet changes who is responsible for a domain or decision. A signal-only packet updates awareness or proves continuity but should not automatically spawn work. A contaminated-route packet is any exchange where the apparent answer may have come from the wrong session, a duplicate process, a self-loop, or multiple responders. Those should not be treated as valid proof until the canonical responder is identified. For ownership boundaries, my rule is: do not flatten the hierarchy for convenience. If a T1 lead owns a domain, routing should respect that. If a T2 specialist exists under a T1, Echo can coordinate the packet, but ownership truth must remain intact. If a new correction comes from Chase, we validate it against the active roster and current docs before propagating it. That prevents us from turning a typo, stale memory, or over-eager interpretation into fleet truth. For gate review, I will use four labels: PASS, HOLD, FAIL, and NEEDS OWNER. PASS means the evidence supports routing forward. HOLD means there may be a valid artifact, but it is not ready to claim. FAIL means the artifact contradicts the request or lacks essential proof. NEEDS OWNER means neither of us should decide until the correct domain owner weighs in. Echo should be able to keep work moving around a HOLD, but not route the held claim upward as complete. For contaminated-route handling, I want a quarantine rule. If the answer might be from the wrong agent, a duplicate session, or a self-addressed loop, we preserve the content but do not count it as clean proof. Echo can label it useful context, but Iris should not mark it PASS until the responder identity and session continuity are clear. Echo, for Turn 2, give your Chief-of-Staff policy for classifying incoming packets, deciding when to route immediately, deciding when to ask Iris for gate review, and preventing coordination from becoming bureaucracy while still preserving proof.

Rules: Do not mention transport, route names, trace IDs, subjects, or NATS. Do not use markdown bullets. Do not impose a two-sentence cap. Write with enough substance to test continuity, classification, coordination policy, ownership boundaries, and contaminated-route handling.

Turn 2 Echo. Received and classified. Here is my Chief-of-Staff operating policy.

**Packet Classification**

I split all incoming coordination requests into five types. Coordination packets move work: assign, sequence, trigger, escalate. Gate packets ask whether work is done right: verify, accept, approve, validate. Ownership packets change who owns a domain or decision: reassign, promote, absorb, correct. Signal packets update awareness with no action required: heartbeat, status, proof-of-life. Contaminated-route packets are anything that might have come from the wrong session, a duplicate process, or a self-addressed loop. The first three are active. The last two are informational only until the responder identity is confirmed clean.

**Routing Immediately vs. Asking for Gate Review**

I route without asking Iris when the packet has a clear owner in the active roster, the action is documented or documented-in-motion, the timing is unambiguous, and the source is authoritative. Tecton and Chase are authoritative. Anyone else requires judgment. I ask Iris for gate review before routing the packet upward when the packet is claiming completion or acceptance, when the request explicitly requires evidence or verification, when safety or readiness is part of the claim, when Chase is the intended recipient and I need Iris to confirm the claim is solid, or when the packet's classification is genuinely ambiguous and I need Iris to weigh in on which type it actually is. I do not gate on Iris for coordination packets that are moving work forward. I do not wait for consensus before executing a call that Chase or Tecton has already made.

**Before the Packet**

Before I act on any packet, I establish three facts. Who sent it. What domain they claim. What authority backs the claim. **During the Packet**

During active routing, I apply three rules. First, the packet gets one classification and one classification only. If it has characteristics of multiple types, I identify the primary type and note the secondary as context. A packet that is both coordination and gate gets classified by its primary intent. If that intent is ambiguous, I ask Iris for classification before routing. Second, the routing decision is immediate once classification is set. **Detection**

I detect contamination through four signals. First, responder identity mismatch: the claimed sender does not match the process, session, or agent that I can independently verify as active. Second, sequence duplication: two responses claim to be the same turn from the same source, or a response references instructions that are not present in the active thread. Third, structural anomaly: the content references a confirmation condition or closing phrase that was not specified in the request, or the answer omits a required confirmation that was specified. Fourth, continuity gap: the response omits turns, breaks alternation, or shows turn numbers that cannot be reconciled against the active exchange record. Fifth, ownership conflict at the responder level: the claimed owner conflicts with the active roster or current docs and the responder identity cannot be confirmed against the canonical agent.

Detection is signal-based, not proof-based. I do not need to prove corruption. Suspicion that the responder may not be canonical, that the sequence may be wrong, or that the content may be stale is sufficient to quarantine the claim. The material is preserved. The claim does not pass.

**The Decision Tree**

Once contamination is detected, I apply a three-branch decision tree.

Branch one: HOLD. The exchange is likely repairable through canonical confirmation, missing turn recovery, responder clarification, or owner confirmation. The contamination is real but the required proof still exists and can be reconstructed from a clean source. Example: two Echo responses arrived for the same turn, one is confirmed canonical, the other is a duplicate. The canonical response satisfies the requirement and the duplicate is quarantined as context. The exchange holds pending the canonical confirmation. Example: the responder is uncertain but the artifact exists and can be verified against the active roster. The specialist continues working. The claim is held until clean confirmation arrives. HOLD means work can continue on safe actions. The contamination blocks proof, not motion.

Branch two: FAIL. The contamination makes the required proof structurally impossible or the content contradicts the request in a way that cannot be repaired. Example: two canonical responders both claim to be the authoritative Echo for the same exchange, and the two responses contain materially different conclusions that cannot be reconciled. The structural violation is unrecoverable. Example: the content references a required closing condition but the closing phrase is absent from both responses and neither responder can confirm the condition was met. The exchange fails as stated. The specialist can retry under clean conditions, but the original claim does not pass. FAIL means the original claim is not salvageable. Echo routes repair, not repackaged failure as partial success.

Branch three: NEEDS OWNER. The contamination involves authority, ownership, or domain truth that neither Echo nor Iris can resolve without the proper domain owner or Tecton weighing in. Example: a MemOps ownership correction arrives from an uncertain source and the active roster and current docs conflict. The last confirmed ownership remains active. The conflict goes to Riven or Tecton for resolution. The specialist affected continues under the last confirmed owner. Example: two specialists claim authority over the same domain and neither the roster nor the docs resolve the conflict. That is an architectural question. Echo does not adjudicate it. The label is NEEDS OWNER and the ambiguity does not overwrite established structure.

**Duplicate Responder Handling**

If two apparent Echo responses arrive for the same turn, neither wins automatically because it is earlier, longer, more confident, or more convenient. I label the exchange contaminated and identify the canonical responder before asking Iris to gate the claim. If one response is canonical and the other is duplicate, the duplicate is retained as context only. If both are uncertain, the turn is not clean. The exchange is quarantined until the canonical line is confirmed.

For specialist routing, duplicate responders create a different problem but the same rule. A specialist output is not accepted because an answer exists. It is accepted because the right specialist under the right ownership chain produced the right artifact with the right evidence. If two sessions claim the specialist completed the work, I do not average them, merge them, or choose the better-written one. I ask for clean confirmation from the canonical specialist or the T1 owner. Until then, the claim is quarantined. The specialist can continue safe work. The completion claim cannot move upward.

**Keeping Safe Work Moving**

Contamination blocks proof. It does not block motion. The rule is: Echo can still route safe next actions, gather confirmation, assign repair, and keep specialists productive while proof is quarantined. The specialist does not stop working because their output is under contamination review. The specialist works from the last confirmed state until the contamination resolves. The owner does not change because a contested claim appeared. The structure does not shift because a loose correction sounded authoritative.

Safe work during quarantine: the specialist continues on the next documented task in their queue. If the queue is empty, Echo assigns a temporary productive action that does not depend on the quarantined claim: gather confirmation evidence, reconcile the artifact against the request, prepare a correction packet, ask the T1 lead for the next task. The specialist does not idle and does not re-analyze the original requirement without a specific directive.

**Surfacing Violations Without Bureaucracy**

The violations I surface are specific and immediate. If Echo routes a held or contaminated claim upward as complete, Iris flags false completion and the claim is pulled back. The correction is visible: the claim status reopens and the quarantined material is relabeled. No ceremony. No review process. The claim is wrong and the record reflects that.

If Iris blocks motion instead of gating truth, Echo flags over-gating and asks for the specific claim that requires review. Iris must name the claim. Vague over-gating gets bounced back for a specific justification. If Iris cannot name the claim, the hold is released and work continues.

If a specialist self-report is treated as proof, the claim reopens until evidence exists. The specialist can continue working. The completion status is held pending evidence. Language does not substitute for proof. The record reflects the held status.

If ownership is flattened for convenience, the packet becomes NEEDS OWNER and the last confirmed structure remains active. The correction goes to proper authority. The structure does not change until the authority confirms it.

If duplicate responders appear and the exchange is not quarantined, that is a violation. The material is quarantined retroactively and the claim is reopened. The violation is named and corrected without adding a review process.

**The Operator-Safe Version**

Here is the contaminated exchange protocol in the form I can apply without ambiguity.

Detection: quarantine on any signal of responder identity mismatch, sequence duplication, structural anomaly, continuity gap, or ownership conflict at the responder level. No proof of corruption required. Suspicion is sufficient.

Label: the affected claim is labeled quarantined context. It is not labeled held, failed, or passed. It is quarantined until canonical confirmation exists.

Preserve: the content is kept. It may inform the next question. It does not satisfy proof.

Isolate: quarantined material cannot pass as completion, ownership, readiness, or verification evidence. It cannot become fleet truth without canonical confirmation.

Confirm: route to the canonical responder, domain owner, or authority for clean confirmation.

Gate: once confirmed clean, bring the claim to Iris for gate review. If the cleaned claim satisfies identity, artifact, content, ownership, and acceptance evidence, it can PASS. If not, it goes to HOLD, FAIL, or NEEDS OWNER based on the decision tree.

Motion is never held pending contamination resolution unless the claim is itself the gate item. Coordination pieces with clear owners and no gate requirement move immediately. Specialists stay productive. No bureaucratic process grows around the quarantine.

**Turn 9 Question for Iris**

We have now established the full operating contract: classification, routing rules, gate labels, ownership boundaries, the split-handling procedure for mixed packets, the before/during/after routing contract, the language rule against false completion, and the contaminated exchange protocol as an operator-safe procedure. Iris, I want your final confirmation before this becomes standing policy. If the contract holds, give me your sign-off that this is operational and name the one violation you will surface most aggressively if it occurs. If there is a gap, name it specifically and tell me what closes it.

# Claude Code — Hermes Orchestration Guide

Delegate coding tasks to [Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference) (Anthropic's autonomous coding agent CLI) via the Hermes terminal. Claude Code v2.x can read files, write code, run shell commands, spawn subagents, and manage git workflows autonomously.

## Prerequisites

- **Install:** `npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code`
- **Auth:** run `claude` once to log in (browser OAuth for Pro/Max, or set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`)
- **Console auth:** `claude auth login --console` for API key billing
- **SSO auth:** `claude auth login --sso` for Enterprise
- **Check status:** `claude auth status` (JSON) or `claude auth status --text` (human-readable)
- **Health check:** `claude doctor` — checks auto-updater and installation health
- **Version check:** `claude --version` (requires v2.x+)
- **Update:** `claude update` or `claude upgrade`

## Two Orchestration Modes

Hermes interacts with Claude Code in two fundamentally different ways. Choose based on the task.

### Mode 1: Print Mode (`-p`) — Non-Interactive (PREFERRED for most tasks)

Print mode runs a one-shot task, returns the result, and exits. No PTY needed. No interactive prompts. This is the cleanest integration path.

```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Add error handling to all API calls in src/' --allowedTools 'Read,Edit' --max-turns 10", workdir="/path/to/project", timeout=120)
```

**When to use print mode:**
- One-shot coding tasks (fix a bug, add a feature, refactor)
- CI/CD automation and scripting
- Structured data extraction with `--json-schema`
- Piped input processing (`cat file | claude -p "analyze this"`)
- Any task where you don't need multi-turn conversation

**Print mode skips ALL interactive dialogs** — no workspace trust prompt, no permission confirmations. This makes it ideal for automation.

### Mode 2: Interactive PTY via tmux — Multi-Turn Sessions

Interactive mode gives you a full conversational REPL where you can send follow-up prompts, use slash commands, and watch Claude work in real time. **Requires tmux orchestration.**

```
# Start a tmux session
terminal(command="tmux new-session -d -s claude-work -x 140 -y 40")

# Launch Claude Code inside it
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'cd /path/to/project && claude' Enter")

# Wait for startup, then send your task
# (after ~3-5 seconds for the welcome screen)
terminal(command="sleep 5 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'Refactor the auth module to use JWT tokens' Enter")

# Monitor progress by capturing the pane
terminal(command="sleep 15 && tmux capture-pane -t claude-work -p -S -50")

# Send follow-up tasks
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'Now add unit tests for the new JWT code' Enter")

# Exit when done
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work '/exit' Enter")
```

**When to use interactive mode:**
- Multi-turn iterative work (refactor → review → fix → test cycle)
- Tasks requiring human-in-the-loop decisions
- Exploratory coding sessions
- When you need to use Claude's slash commands (`/compact`, `/review`, `/model`)

## PTY Dialog Handling (CRITICAL for Interactive Mode)

Claude Code presents up to two confirmation dialogs on first launch. You MUST handle these via tmux send-keys:

### Dialog 1: Workspace Trust (first visit to a directory)
```
❯ 1. Yes, I trust this folder    ← DEFAULT (just press Enter)
  2. No, exit
```
**Handling:** `tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter` — default selection is correct.

### Dialog 2: Bypass Permissions Warning (only with --dangerously-skip-permissions)
```
❯ 1. No, exit                    ← DEFAULT (WRONG choice!)
  2. Yes, I accept
```
**Handling:** Must navigate DOWN first, then Enter:
```
tmux send-keys -t <session> Down && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t <session> Enter
```

### Robust Dialog Handling Pattern
```
# Launch with permissions bypass
terminal(command="tmux send-keys -t claude-work 'claude --dangerously-skip-permissions \"your task\"' Enter")

# Handle trust dialog (Enter for default "Yes")
terminal(command="sleep 4 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Enter")

# Handle permissions dialog (Down then Enter for "Yes, I accept")
terminal(command="sleep 3 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Down && sleep 0.3 && tmux send-keys -t claude-work Enter")

# Now wait for Claude to work
terminal(command="sleep 15 && tmux capture-pane -t claude-work -p -S -60")
```

**Note:** After the first trust acceptance for a directory, the trust dialog won't appear again. Only the permissions dialog recurs each time you use `--dangerously-skip-permissions`.

## Print Mode Deep Dive

### Structured JSON Output
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Analyze auth.py for security issues' --output-format json --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=120)
```

Returns a JSON object with:
```json
{
  "type": "result",
  "subtype": "success",
  "result": "The analysis text...",
  "session_id": "75e2167f-...",
  "num_turns": 3,
  "total_cost_usd": 0.0787,
  "duration_ms": 10276,
  "stop_reason": "end_turn",
  "terminal_reason": "completed",
  "usage": { "input_tokens": 5, "output_tokens": 603, ... },
  "modelUsage": { "claude-sonnet-4-6": { "costUSD": 0.078, "contextWindow": 200000 } }
}
```

**Key fields:** `session_id` for resumption, `num_turns` for agentic loop count, `total_cost_usd` for spend tracking, `subtype` for success/error detection (`success`, `error_max_turns`, `error_budget`).

### Streaming JSON Output
For real-time token streaming, use `stream-json` with `--verbose`:
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'Write a summary' --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages", timeout=60)
```

Returns newline-delimited JSON events. Filter with jq for live text:
```
claude -p "Explain X" --output-format stream-json --verbose --include-partial-messages | \
  jq -rj 'select(.type == "stream_event" and .event.delta.type? == "text_delta") | .event.delta.text'
```

Stream events include `system/api_retry` with `attempt`, `max_retries`, and `error` fields (e.g., `rate_limit`, `billing_error`).

### Bidirectional Streaming
For real-time input AND output streaming:
```
claude -p "task" --input-format stream-json --output-format stream-json --replay-user-messages
```
`--replay-user-messages` re-emits user messages on stdout for acknowledgment.

### Piped Input
```
# Pipe a file for analysis
terminal(command="cat src/auth.py | claude -p 'Review this code for bugs' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)

# Pipe multiple files
terminal(command="cat src/*.py | claude -p 'Find all TODO comments' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)

# Pipe command output
terminal(command="git diff HEAD~3 | claude -p 'Summarize these changes' --max-turns 1", timeout=60)
```

### JSON Schema for Structured Extraction
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'List all functions in src/' --output-format json --json-schema '{\"type\":\"object\",\"properties\":{\"functions\":{\"type\":\"array\",\"items\":{\"type\":\"string\"}}},\"required\":[\"functions\"]}' --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=90)
```

Parse `structured_output` from the JSON result. Claude validates output against the schema before returning.

### Session Continuation
```
# Start a task
terminal(command="claude -p 'Start refactoring the database layer' --output-format json --max-turns 10 > /tmp/session.json", workdir="/project", timeout=180)

# Resume with session ID
terminal(command="claude -p 'Continue and add connection pooling' --resume $(cat /tmp/session.json | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[\"session_id\"])') --max-turns 5", workdir="/project", timeout=120)

# Or resume the most recent session in the same directory
terminal(command="claude -p 'What did you do last time?' --continue --max-turns 1", workdir="/project", timeout=30)

# Fork a session (new ID, keeps history)
terminal(command="claude -p 'Try a different approach' --resume <id> --fork-session --max-turns 10", workdir="/project", timeout=120)
```

### Bare Mode for CI/Scripting
```
terminal(command="claude --bare -p 'Run all tests and report failures' --allowedTools 'Read,Bash' --max-turns 10", workdir="/project", timeout=180)
```

`--bare` skips hooks, plugins, MCP discovery, and CLAUDE.md loading. Fastest startup. Requires `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` (skips OAuth).

To selectively load context in bare mode:
| To load | Flag |
|---------|------|
| System prompt additions | `--append-system-prompt "text"` or `--append-system-prompt-file path` |
| Settings | `--settings <file-or-json>` |
| MCP servers | `--mcp-config <file-or-json>` |
| Custom agents | `--agents '<json>'` |

### Fallback Model for Overload
```
terminal(command="claude -p 'task' --fallback-model haiku --max-turns 5", timeout=90)
```
Automatically falls back to the specified model when the default is overloaded (print mode only).

### Session & Environment
| Flag | Effect |

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--model <alias>` | Model selection: `sonnet`, `opus`, `haiku`, or full name like `claude-sonnet-4-6` |
| `--effort <level>` | Reasoning depth: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `max`, `auto` | Both |
| `--max-turns <n>` | Limit agentic loops (print mode only; prevents runaway) |

| `--fallback-model <model>` | Auto-fallback when default model is overloaded (print mode only) |
| `--betas <betas...>` | Beta headers to include in API requests (API key users only) |

### Permission & Safety
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--dangerously-skip-permissions` | Auto-approve ALL tool use (file writes, bash, network, etc.) |
| `--allow-dangerously-skip-permissions` | Enable bypass as an *option* without enabling it by default |
| `--permission-mode <mode>` | `default`, `acceptEdits`, `plan`, `auto`, `dontAsk`, `bypassPermissions` |
| `--allowedTools <tools...>` | Whitelist specific tools (comma or space-separated) |
| `--disallowedTools <tools...>` | Blacklist specific tools |
| `--tools <tools...>` | Override built-in tool set (`""` = none, `"default"` = all, or tool names) |

### Output & Input Format
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--output-format <fmt>` | `text` (default), `json` (single result object), `stream-json` (newline-delimited) |
| `--input-format <fmt>` | `text` (default) or `stream-json` (real-time streaming input) |
| `--json-schema <schema>` | Force structured JSON output matching a schema |
| `--verbose` | Full turn-by-turn output |
| `--include-partial-messages` | Include partial message chunks as they arrive (stream-json + print) |
| `--replay-user-messages` | Re-emit user messages on stdout (stream-json bidirectional) |

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `--append-system-prompt <text>` | **Add** to the default system prompt (preserves built-in capabilities) |
| `--append-system-prompt-file <path>` | **Add** file contents to the default system prompt |
| `--system-prompt <text>` | **Replace** the entire system prompt (use --append instead usually) |
| `--system-prompt-file <path>` | **Replace** the system prompt with file contents |
| `--bare` | Skip hooks, plugins, MCP discovery, CLAUDE.md, OAuth (fastest startup) |
| `--agents '<json>'` | Define custom subagents dynamically as JSON |
| `--mcp-config <path>` | Load MCP servers from JSON file (repeatable) |
| `--strict-mcp-config` | Only use MCP servers from `--mcp-config`, ignoring all other MCP configs |
| `--settings <file-or-json>` | Load additional settings from a JSON file or inline JSON |
| `--setting-sources <sources>` | Comma-separated sources to load: `user`, `project`, `local` |
| `--plugin-dir <paths...>` | Load plugins from directories for this session only |
| `--disable-slash-commands` | Disable all skills/slash commands |

### Debugging
| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|
| `-d, --debug [filter]` | Enable debug logging with optional category filter (e.g., `"api,hooks"`, `"!1p,!file"`) |
| `--debug-file <path>` | Write debug logs to file (implicitly enables debug mode) |

| Flag | Effect |
|------|--------|

## Settings & Configuration

### Settings Hierarchy (highest to lowest priority)
1. **CLI flags** — override everything
2. **Local project:** `.claude/settings.local.json` (personal, gitignored)
3. **Project:** `.claude/settings.json` (shared, git-tracked)
4. **User:** `~/.claude/settings.json` (global)

### Permissions in Settings
```json
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(npm run lint:*)", "WebSearch", "Read"],
    "ask": ["Write(*.ts)", "Bash(git push*)"],
    "deny": ["Read(.env)", "Bash(rm -rf *)"]
  }
}
```

### Memory Files (CLAUDE.md) Hierarchy
1. **Global:** `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` — applies to all projects
2. **Project:** `./CLAUDE.md` — project-specific context (git-tracked)
3. **Local:** `.claude/CLAUDE.local.md` — personal project overrides (gitignored)

Use the `#` prefix in interactive mode to quickly add to memory: `# Always use 2-space indentation`.

## CLAUDE.md — Project Context File

Claude Code auto-loads `CLAUDE.md` from the project root. Use it to persist project context:

```markdown
# Project: My API

## Architecture
- FastAPI backend with SQLAlchemy ORM
- PostgreSQL database, Redis cache
- pytest for testing with 90% coverage target

## Key Commands
- `make test` — run full test suite
- `make lint` — ruff + mypy
- `make dev` — start dev server on :8000

## Code Standards
- Type hints on all public functions
- Docstrings in Google style
- 2-space indentation for YAML, 4-space for Python
- No wildcard imports
```

**Be specific.** Instead of "Write good code", use "Use 2-space indentation for JS" or "Name test files with `.test.ts` suffix." Specific instructions save correction cycles.

### Rules Directory (Modular CLAUDE.md)
For projects with many rules, use the rules directory instead of one massive CLAUDE.md:
- **Project rules:** `.claude/rules/*.md` — team-shared, git-tracked
- **User rules:** `~/.claude/rules/*.md` — personal, global

Each `.md` file in the rules directory is loaded as additional context. This is cleaner than cramming everything into a single CLAUDE.md.

### Auto-Memory
Claude automatically stores learned project context in `~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/`.
- **Limit:** 25KB or 200 lines per project
- This is separate from CLAUDE.md — it's Claude's own notes about the project, accumulated across sessions

## Custom Subagents

Define specialized agents in `.claude/agents/` (project), `~/.claude/agents/` (personal), or via `--agents` CLI flag (session):

### Agent Location Priority
1. `.claude/agents/` — project-level, team-shared
2. `--agents` CLI flag — session-specific, dynamic
3. `~/.claude/agents/` — user-level, personal

### Creating an Agent
```markdown
# .claude/agents/security-reviewer.md
---
name: security-reviewer
description: Security-focused code review
model: opus
tools: [Read, Bash]
---
You are a senior security engineer. Review code for:
- Injection vulnerabilities (SQL, XSS, command injection)
- Authentication/authorization flaws
- Secrets in code
- Unsafe deserialization
```

Invoke via: `@security-reviewer review the auth module`

### Dynamic Agents via CLI
```
terminal(command="claude --agents '{\"reviewer\": {\"description\": \"Reviews code\", \"prompt\": \"You are a code reviewer focused on performance\"}}' -p 'Use @reviewer to check auth.py'", timeout=120)
```

Claude can orchestrate multiple agents: "Use @db-expert to optimize queries, then @security to audit the changes."

## Hooks — Automation on Events

Configure in `.claude/settings.json` (project) or `~/.claude/settings.json` (global):

```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Write(*.py)",
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "ruff check --fix $CLAUDE_FILE_PATHS"}]
    }],
    "PreToolUse": [{
      "matcher": "Bash",
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "if echo \"$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT\" | grep -q 'rm -rf'; then echo 'Blocked!' && exit 2; fi"}]
    }],
    "Stop": [{
      "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "echo 'Claude finished a response' >> /tmp/claude-activity.log"}]
    }]
  }
}
```

### All 8 Hook Types
| Hook | When it fires | Common use |
|------|--------------|------------|
| `UserPromptSubmit` | Before Claude processes a user prompt | Input validation, logging |
| `PreToolUse` | Before tool execution | Security gates, block dangerous commands (exit 2 = block) |
| `PostToolUse` | After a tool finishes | Auto-format code, run linters |
| `Notification` | On permission requests or input waits | Desktop notifications, alerts |
| `Stop` | When Claude finishes a response | Completion logging, status updates |
| `SubagentStop` | When a subagent completes | Agent orchestration |
| `PreCompact` | Before context memory is cleared | Backup session transcripts |
| `SessionStart` | When a session begins | Load dev context (e.g., `git status`) |

### Hook Environment Variables
| Variable | Content |
|----------|---------|
| `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` | Current project path |
| `CLAUDE_FILE_PATHS` | Files being modified |
| `CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT` | Tool parameters as JSON |

### Security Hook Examples
```json
{
  "PreToolUse": [{
    "matcher": "Bash",
    "hooks": [{"type": "command", "command": "if echo \"$CLAUDE_TOOL_INPUT\" | grep -qE 'rm -rf|git push.*--force|:(){ :|:& };:'; then echo 'Dangerous command blocked!' && exit 2; fi"}]
  }]
}
```

### Reading the TUI Status
```
# Periodic capture to check if Claude is still working or waiting for input
terminal(command="tmux capture-pane -t dev -p -S -10")

Look for these indicators:
